newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's budget forecasts 1997/98 deficit C$17 bln.
newsitem.headline: Canada's budget forecasts 1997/98 deficit C$17 bln.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin on Tuesday made the following forecasts in the fiscal 1997/98 budget (figures in billions of Canadian dollars):
Program spending 109.0 (R)105.8 103.5
Public debt charges (R)45.5 (R)46.0 46.5
Underlying deficit (R)19.0 (R)14.0 6.0
Contingency reserve (R) nil 3.0 3.0
Deficit as pct of GDP (R)2.4 2.0 1.0
Financial requirement 6.0 6.0 6.0
Net public debt 593.3 610.3 619.3
Net public debt (pct of GDP) 74.4 73.1 71.2

NOTE: Canada's fiscal year runs from April 1 through March 31. Financial requirement excludes foreign exchange requirements and is considered a comprehensive measure of the government's borrowing in credit markets.

The 1996/97 estimated deficit of no more than C$19.0 billion was C$5.0 billion below the C$24.3 billion Martin projected in his previous budget and C$9.6 billion below the 1995/96 deficit, the largest year-over-year decline ever.

Martin repeated on Tuesday that he would eventually eliminate the deficit, but stopped short of setting a date for that. Instead, he said he would stick to the two-year rolling targets he used in the 1995/96 and 1996/97 budgets.

"We will balance the books. We will do so by maintaining our pace - deliberate, measured and responsible," Martin said in his budget speech to Parliament. "We will maintain our approach of two-year rolling targets. And we will not alter the course."

Martin repeated his pledge to bring Canada's borrowing requirement down to zero in 1998/99, the first time in 28 years. This will eliminate the need for new borrowing in financial markets to pay for government programs and interest on Canada's debt.
Noting that many G7 countries use borrowing requirements as the measure of their deficits, Martin said Canada is poised for a small surplus in 1998/99 by that measure.

"According to this measure, by 1998/99 Canada is expected to have a small surplus, and the best financial record of any of the seven largest industrialized countries," Martin said. "This is a turnaround of unprecedented proportions."

Martin also forecast a decline in Canada's debt-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio in 1997/98. He said his government's goal was to put the debt-to-GDP ratio on a "permanent downward track" for the first time in over 20 years.

There were no new taxes and no new cuts to government programs in the budget. Instead, Martin pledged to spend C$1 billion in targeted tax relief and new program spending in 1997/98, together with C$800 million for a new project to modernize research facilities and equipment at universities and hospitals.
Federal government program spending was forecast to drop to C$103.5 billion by 1998/99 from C$120 billion in 1993/94.

Martin eliminated the C$2.5 billion contingency reserve he had budgeted for 1996/97 and revised his program spending projections for 1997/98 down to C$105.8 billion from the C$106.0 billion he had forecast in a budget update last October.
The budget also forecast an operating balance, the difference between budget revenues and program spending, of C$32.0 billion in 1997/98 and C$40.5 billion in 1998/99.
Martin based his forecasts on the assumption that Canada's economy would grow 3.2 percent in 1997 and 2.6 percent in 1998 and inflation would be 1.5 percent in both years.
((Malina Poshtova Zang, Reuters Ottawa Bureau, 613-235-6745))
